title: Unforgiven (1992) - Everyone thinks they're the man...

commenti.body: [removed]

Great film. William being so horrible and yet you give him your absolute full support every time. It helps that everybody else has terrible flaws too, but to pull support for pretty much Satan himself sets this film apart from any other. 

Where else would you watch an ex alcoholic child and woman murderer and wish him to go back on the booze because he's too nervous to fight sober.
[removed]

Yep. And the scene where he goes back on the booze when he hears what they've done to Ned - you barely notice it. They don't try and magnify it with music or anything. He's already halfway through the bottle before you realise: oh shit, he's drinking again. We know what's about to come.

And after the kid kills the guy in the outhouse, all Munny has to offer is: "Take a drink of that whiskey." He knows the kid is probably set for a life of all the same torture and trouble he's had.
[removed]

It is interesting that Little Bill enjoys showing off to Mr. Beauchamp (the always stellar Saul Rubenik).


First, he makes him piss his pants in fear.  


Then, the whole sequence in the jail cell.  When Beauchamp is unwilling to shoot, he asks what if he gave the gun to English Bob?


You can practically feel Little Bill sprout a semi at the suggestion.


Just a few scenes later, when they're torturing Ned, Beauchamp is now a trusted advisor.


When Ned contradicts his story, Beauchamp has the notes, and merely shakes his head at Little Bill.


Bill enjoys having his ego stroked, even though he knows and admits he's not the fastest on the draw.  He just thinks he's smarter, more vicious, more in command.


There is this incredibly small moment near the beginning, where the saloon keeper rides out to tell him about the bounty, and at first he seems genuinely shocked one of his guys was just out to pay a visit.


Always found that little moment funny, but it's telling about his ego.

Yes, there's also Bill's insecurity about his carpentry work that ties into this. There are enough little moments like that which let us know he's actually quite fragile, and that underneath all his bravado, he's not very unlike English Bob.

There's also a moment with Munny that feeds into this. Munny and Ned are talking about their old gang, and Munny notes that none of them really liked him; they were all just afraid that he might shoot them at any moment. 

Munny accepts his predicament, his lack of friends, the hatred he invokes in everyone around him. Whereas Bill has to fool himself to some extent.

Hackman's character of Herrod in *The Quick and the Dead* is basically a fully realized version of Little Bill.


He really is that fast, that deadly, that feared.  Ace Hanlon was just an even more foppish oaf than English Bob, with all the complexity and ambiguity stripped away.

I think your take is entirely valid.

I will say this and consider this a mild disagreement, I consider English Bob to be more of an extreme version of William Munny,   someone who has heavy baggage from decades earlier.

I actually believe that unfair punishment and wacked  out scales of justice is the theme of this movie. 

The slap on the wrist of the initial perpetrators of the woman who gets her face slashed up, to the brutal whipping of Morgan Freeman's character, who while an accomplice,  hasn't really participated in the activities of William and the Kid.

So going back to English Bob, in theory this might be the only time Little Bill was able to effectively pick on a "deserving" victim.

However cinematically speaking, it's a middle-aged guy beating up an old man. 

So I actually think William Munny did do worse things than Little Bill in his lifetime, but without seeing any of his real outlaw past on screen, it feels as if a necessary evil is confronting a gleeful one. 

I am kind of annoyed at the term revisionist Western, because I do think most celebrated Westerns post Stagecoach are psychological dramas which go against the run of the mill approaches of countless Western heroes. 

But I will say that Unforgiven is a Mount Rushmore Western, taking the viciousness of the Old Spaghetti Westerns ( first hand experience, heh) and blending it with the more morally ambiguous films that you might see in the seventies pre-star Wars.   

Cinematography is also out of the world, feeling more Gorda Willis-ish than glamorous. A classic in every sense of the word.

Good point on the theme of unfair punishment and the lack of, or even random, justice.

It's driven home by the final scene between Bill and Munny. Little Bill, lying on the floor dying, says: "I don't deserve to die like this."

Munny replies: "Deserve's got nothin' to do with it." 

Then pulls the trigger.

Sorry, but Bill torturing Ned reveals him to be every bit as bad as Munny… his attention to carpentry does not absolve him of this - in fact, it makes him more insidious, and shows how evil can be present in the most mundane places and in the seemingly most normal of people.

My point about the carpentry was to show Bill's ego still gets the better of him. It had nothing to do with absolving his evil-doings. Sorry if I was unclear about that.

From a lawman's perspective, Bill whipped Ned to stop any further bloodshed in his town - rightly or wrongly.

When Munny blew up a train full of women and children, he had no such excuse to lean on - and wanted none. He simply did not care.

“I think your take is entirely valid.”

“Munny is not a hero of any kind. If anything, the closest thing to a 'good guy' here is Little Bill.”

This just doesn’t jibe right with me. I can see you’re trying to go deep into it but this is too much 😆 

Just because Litte Bill’s on the side of the “law” doesn’t make him good.

The slap on the wrist of the initial perpetrators of the woman who gets her face slashed up, to the brutal whipping of Morgan Freeman's character, who while an accomplice, hasn't really participated in the activities of William and the Kid.”

Yeah he tortures and executes Ned. Quiet, timid, Morgan Freeman.

I get that Munny was a murderer, and there’s a mythos surrounding his youth, but we don’t see him do anything reprehensible in the film. Calling him evil incarnate and “Satan” is silly.

The film is a lot of things but to me, based on the intro and outro, it’s about redemption and whether or not we can forgive ourselves.

Films are about many things. I simply wrote about what stood out to me. It's absolutely about redemption and whether or not we can forgive ourselves.

Nobody said Little Bill was good. I said he was the closest thing. In a film filled with reprehensible characters, that isn't saying much.

>Later, when Munny confronts Little Bill, we see that everything Little Bill said was true - but also that he himself doesn't necessarily have it. Munny is the personification of the calm, composed man he was talking about - but crucially, it's not presented as 'cool' or virtuous.

Also, crucially, everything that Little Bill and English Bob say is disproven by Munny's actions. At the end of the gunfight in the bar the writer asks him who he shot first, explaining that Bill claimed when faced by superior numbers a gunslinger will always go for the best shot first. But those truisms don't actually hold any water, they're just sayings that old men make up to give themselves some semblance of order or meaning in what they've done. Munny replies, "I was lucky in the order, but I've always been lucky when it comes to killing folks". He wins the fight, and not because of some hard-earned logic of the West, he wins because he's lucky. 

Munny shows how there is no order or justice in that world ("Deserves got nothing to do with it", etc.), it's just luck and whoever is willing to be the most ruthless. It doesn't just dismantle the grand idea of a moral cowboy saving the small outpost with his superior morality, it also takes apart the idea that even an anti-hero will rise to the top. The frontier is random, and amoral, there is no logic to it, and those who try to impose order onto it will end up dead on the floor just as easily as victorious in the gun fight.

Well said. For a brief moment we get the feeling the writer might attach himself to Munny, but Munny soon puts paid to that by threatening to kill him. He has no interest in his own mythology because, as you point out, he can see through all of that nonsense.

I just watched this this week for the first time since I saw it in the theater when I was 17. I remember enjoying the movie but not thinking it was anything that would become an all time classic. It was just a good action movie to me.

Seeing it now, 34 years later,  with almost three times the life experience, and having seen a million more westerns, since, the movie's brilliance is unmistakable. 

It's a revisionist western, but also one that is fully part of the western genre, it's meta-commentary while also a straight, satisfying narrative. 

What the movie manages to pull off in the ending is especially deft. You get the cathartic revenge scene that powers so many westerns. We get to cheer along while our hero murders a bunch of people and says bad-ass one liners, while at the same time,  the actual violence, the actual moral blankness, the actual devastation, is also  clear and overwhelming.

There are just so many aspects that just work so perfectly. It is indeed an all-time classic.

I was really happy to see this thread because just rewatched it yesterday. Said that, youve written an interesting text which I surely valued, so dont mind me disagreeing with some parts.

>Later, when Munny confronts Little Bill, we see that everything Little Bill said was true - but also that he himself doesn't necessarily have it. Munny is the personification of the calm, composed man he was talking about - but crucially, it's not presented as 'cool' or virtuous. The reason Munny is so good at this is because he's without ego, without principle, almost entirely evil. In other words, the very kind of man who would survive in the old west. 

In which sense you are using the term 'ego'? It doesnt seem to make sense within buddhists, Jungs or Freuds definition.

Ego is not principle or anything similar to none. Even in the popularized conotation of the word, it would describe 'vanity' or a self centered human being. Which is the opposite of what was put here.

The fact that he took personally Neds death, and its taking revenge on it, evidences the opposite thru all the mentioned lenses. The fact that he had to drink to do it too.

To me, if anything at all, the movie describes much more modern ideogical themes. No one was against bloodshed, Little Bill did tried to diminish it, but by making women, hookers and a black man pay the heavier price. Men of the law, who were reinforcing order, were the villains. Means, revolution is needed. And a murderer of innocent men, women and children, was the hero. A repented one who respected black men, indian women (Neds wife) and oppressed women. Thru neo-marxists lenses, the lumpenproletariat are not also allies, but agents of revolution against oppression.

So the theme is too a mixed of ideological views. Authoritarian order becomes evil and only criminal bringing chaos can liberate people. No guns allowed, only for the law men who abused their power, while respecting each other but oppressing women. Feminism, the right to bear a firearm. Its a mix, just like in most Eastwood movies. He always brings conservative views interleaved with progressive ones. Like it or not, nuanced. Cry Macho, The Mule, J. Edgar, Invictus, Millon Dollar Baby, Gran Torino, and so on.

Like I said in another post, Eastwood brings conservative themes mixed with progressive ones.

A black man, who married an indian strong woman, goes with his partner to punish authoritarian patriarchal order. Ex-criminals, heavy ones, lumpenproletariat. The black man is tortured till death. Racism. The white man who cutted the hooker is not even whipped, he just has to repay the owner of the brothel with new horses. Means, women are objects, no human value, specially hookers. Lumpenproletariat again and feminism. The Kid too, he is bold to some extent but innocent. The youth, the black movement and the criminal against oppression.

English Bob is humiliated, he is a liar and even coward. Shot a man who was defenseless just because he had bigger genitals than him and used it to had sex with a woman Bob was in love. The english also provokes just to humiliate, the faisons shooting. He also is a hard defender of monarchy, its important to him. Means conservativism is a lie, based on patriarchy ran by men with weak egos.

Little Bill too, he loves giving big speeches, even risk giving a loaded gun to two men he arrested and humiliated. Even adopts later one of them to write his biography. He is so vain that almost loses his temper when the writer makes a joke about him beimg a bad carpenter. Vanity, weak egos again. Authoritarian weak egos. But he doesnt care if the hooker was cut, to him she is a mere object.

The reason why Delilah was cut was because she laughed about the clients small genitals. Male frailty again, weak egos. The hookers also pay the outlaw with romanceless meaningless sex, suffrage, feminism, to use sex as a revolutionary tool.

William at first struggles to mount the angry horse. He states to his children that its because he cursed and mistreated animals in the past. Animals rights.

Interestingly, the movie essentially comes full circle. While Munny can be seen as the final debunking of myth, as Little Bill debunked English Bob, he's simultaneously uplifted and protected by myth.

At the end, if you count, he shoots six times. Everyone who's too scared to finish him off is being intimidated by a man with an empty gun, because they think he's the devil himself.

Combined with his fire and brimstone threats, with the American flag in the background, and the film's little bookend,

"And there was nothing on the marker to explain to Mrs. Feathers why her only daughter had married a known thief and murderer, a man of notoriously vicious and intemperate disposition."

to me it's clearly not meant as a full blown deconstruction of Westerns.

The dead wife is symbolic of the film's audience, who's now seen an ugly "real" portrayal of Westerns, but is also meant to, I think, understand what they love about them/Munny.

In the final shootout, Little Bill actually draws his pistol before Munny, be he panic fires and misses, while Munny calmly takes a knee and lands every shot, killing five men. When the writer questions him about who he shot first, he says he was lucky in the order, but then again he was always lucky when it came to killing. This dialogue shows both his lack of ego, and the very real nature of this kind of life he's led. The movie is absolutely brilliant.

> I am kind of annoyed at the term revisionist Western, because I do think most celebrated Westerns post Stagecoach are psychological dramas which go against the run of the mill approaches of countless Western heroes.

I think that's a fair timeline but that it just means the revisionist Western got off to an early start. It's not like there isn't a big corpus of pre-revisionist material. Tropes of the Wild West go back further than cinema, as this film examines.

Yeah, I referred to lack of ego in the context of Little Bill's previous speech about gunslingers coming into a bar and acting tough. Munny clearly isn't one of those guys. 

I do agree with your point. Ned's death does wake something up in him. But in the final shootout, he's simply there to kill. He doesn't deliver any grand speeches. I'm using 'ego' in absolute layman's terms here.
Interesting analysis. I don't typically look at films through a purely Marxist lens, but you've given me something to think about.

Yes. The irony of all the townsfolk buying into the myth of Munny - which he doesn't even believe in himself - is so sweet.

The final scene bookend you mention is very impactful. Up until that point, we're left with quite a cynical feeling, and would even be quite happy with it. But when we see quote about the wife it brings us back round.

I always saw Munny as just the guy willing to do it more than anything along with people's sense of self preservation a whole town wasn't going to step in. He's not an action movie star but rather people are naturally scared. There's many scenes where the contract killers take advantage of that like the outhouse Munny simply covered the boy by blasting his shot gun he controlled many men with guns. Even when they come out bravely as they're riding away they're shooting so panicked and erratically they couldn't have hit anything they're still worried about returned fire. Or when Munny is just blasting away in Curlys bar and kills little bill. 

There's a lot myths being destroyed in the movie like how in the end the righteous peace maker paid to right the wrongs after the fact is just this guy willing to take the money. Or I also really liked how most involved were sort of losers. little bill was bringing up men of character but it looked like even he had really nothing going on in his life, even his house he is proud of is all messed up and built poorly.

* Piggybacking on what you said, my argument there wasn't itself that Stagecoach is a revisionist Western, ( I think films like Stagecoach and Shane or even the Magnificent Seven (John Sturges) are sentimentally driven love lettets to the period setting, heroic cowboy, saloon bartenders, etc. I also consider them to be masterful movies.

But I also think that films like Red River, The Searchers, The Naked Spur and High Noon are indictments of the masculine driven fascism of the Wild West ( and are arguably themselves revisionist westerns)

My frustration is that this particular term is usually applied to Westerns post 70s, which subversively creates this feeling that earlier Westerns are these cheery one dimensional narratives.

But you know, when there's over  2000 westerns, it's easy to draw flawed conclusions 😉

Appreciate this thread as I actually watched this film for the first time about a week ago. 

One thing that stuck with me was the scene where Munny leaves the saloon, yells at the town, then rides off with the whores watching. 

The whole nature of the bounty was enacting revenge that Delilah didn't even seem to want. when the "accomplice" comes back with his partner after the thaw to bring his 2 horses plus an additional one for Delilah, she seems to genuinely be touched by the gesture. The whores don't accept his gift and they chase him out of town insisting on getting their revenge. From my recollection they don't ever stop to ask Delilah to ask if that's what she wants. 

When you place an ad looking for a killer who actually shows up at the end? A killer like William Munny. 

A man who says if he sees anyone in the street he's not only killing them, but their family and friends as well, and burning down their house too. 

------------------------------------------

Another thing about this movie is it makes us as the audience essentially complicit in Munny's fall from grace. 

I'm sure some people might claim differently, but in your heart of heart when Munny shows up to the saloon to enact revenge, say some badass lines, the first instinct is to think it's pretty badass. The action in the movie so far has been very tame by Western standards, and now we get the big shootout in the saloon. 

That's why this movie is such a great deconstruction.

I don't really have anything to add here, but I just wanted to leave a comment because your analysis made me look at Unforgiven and the rest of Eastwood's modern filmography through a slightly different lens. Appreciate it.
Youre welcome!
